title: In crises, harmful information is becoming an operational hazard that can determine aid access, safety, dignity, trust, and recovery
source_unit: IFRC World Disasters Report 2026: Truth, Trust and Humanitarian Action in the Age of Harmful Information
geography: Global humanitarian operations and communities affected by disasters, public-health emergencies, migration, and conflict

denominator.unit: organizations contributing written insights to the report, including more than 30 National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

harmful_information_status.value: Harmful information is framed as a de facto humanitarian crisis that undermines aid access, erodes trust, misleads communities, deepens vulnerability, and destabilizes social cohesion

scope.value: Misinformation, disinformation, dehumanizing narratives, rumours, myths, and propaganda moving across online and offline channels

operational_effect.value: Information reliability is treated as part of preparedness, response, recovery, acceptance, safety, and principled humanitarian action

observations.method: IFRC flagship report synthesis drawing on nearly 100 written contributions from more than 60 practitioners and researchers across humanitarian organizations, governments, academia, civil society, and related fields.
observations.uncertainty: This is a sector synthesis and operational risk assessment, not a global prevalence estimate or a single causal study; the term harmful information is intentionally impact-focused and context-dependent rather than a universally standardized classification.
observations.subgroup: People affected by disasters, public-health emergencies, migration, and conflict; humanitarian staff and volunteers; local leaders; governments; media; technology companies; and civil-society organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Information can also guide people to safety, connect families, support community voice, and improve accountability; harmful effects vary by trust, channel, context, access, language, and institutional conduct.

observations.period: 2026 report; community intelligence study for the World Disasters Report

denominator.unit: volunteers and community members affected by humanitarian crises interviewed in the report's rapid community intelligence study

researchers.unit: volunteers and staff from 10 National Societies acting as community researchers

community_input.value: Local perspectives were collected and synthesized to preserve community nuance in the report's analysis of harmful information and trust

localization_signal.value: Trust, feedback, local voices, and community participation are treated as operational capacities rather than merely communication outputs

observations.method: Two-month rapid community intelligence study led by the IFRC Solferino Academy; 40 volunteers and staff from 10 National Societies interviewed 132 affected volunteers and community members, with synthesis by volunteer academics from three universities.
observations.uncertainty: The study is purposive and qualitative, not representative of all affected populations or crises; its value is contextual insight and local nuance, not prevalence or population-level effect estimation.
observations.subgroup: Volunteers, staff, community members affected by humanitarian crises, National Societies, local leaders, and researchers supporting community-informed response.
observations.counterinterpretation: Community participation can be uneven or risky in polarized environments; local voices may be excluded, co-opted, exposed to retaliation, or treated as symbolic without decision power and feedback loops.

observations.period: 2024-2025; Red Cross and Red Crescent duty-of-care context reported in the 2026 foreword

denominator.unit: IFRC report foreword's staff and volunteer safety account

2024_deaths.unit: Red Cross and Red Crescent volunteers and staff reported killed while on duty in 2024

2025_deaths.unit: additional volunteers and staff reported killed while on duty in 2025

information_security_link.value: The report links mistrust, hostility, inflammatory narratives, and attacks on the protective emblem to the operational space needed by humanitarian personnel

observations.method: Counts and interpretation reproduced from the IFRC Secretary General's foreword in the official report synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: The foreword's counts are not a complete global accounting of all humanitarian-worker deaths or a causal attribution to harmful information; the report uses them to illustrate duty-of-care and trust risks.
observations.subgroup: Humanitarian volunteers and staff, affected communities, local partners, armed and political actors, media, and institutions responsible for protecting humanitarian access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Worker deaths arise from multiple hazards including conflict, crime, accidents, and unsafe environments; information harm may compound risk without being the primary cause in each case.

observations.period: 2026 report; resilience roadmap for humanitarian information environments

denominator.unit: core pillars in the IFRC roadmap for resilience against harmful information

trust_as_asset.value: Trust is identified as a strategic asset supporting access, operational effectiveness, delivery, and legitimacy

resilience_actions.value: The roadmap embeds trust, community engagement and accountability, safer access, programme design, preparedness, risk management, communication, data transparency, local voices, and feedback

trust_continuum.value: Trust is described as something that must be repeatedly earned and demonstrated: tell me, show me, prove it, keep proving it

observations.method: IFRC synthesis of eight roadmap pillars and cross-cutting prerequisites for short-, medium-, and longer-term humanitarian resilience.
observations.uncertainty: The roadmap is a normative and operational framework; it does not by itself demonstrate implementation, resource sufficiency, or improved outcomes across humanitarian contexts.
observations.subgroup: States, humanitarian organizations, technology companies, media, communities, local leaders, donors, and data and accountability teams.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trust-building can become a messaging exercise if organizations do not change conduct, share control, address grievances, protect data, and demonstrate visible accountability.

related_sources.claim: Official IFRC landing page describes the report's scope, contributors, crisis settings, and downloadable synthesis and chapters.

boundary: This record adds a humanitarian information-resilience signal linking misinformation, disinformation, dehumanizing narratives, trust, aid access, safety, social cohesion, local participation, and data systems. It is a sector synthesis and operational roadmap, not a global prevalence study, a causal estimate of information effects, a representative community survey, or proof that the recommended pillars are implemented or effective everywhere.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official IFRC World Disasters Report 2026 synthesis PDF reviewed for contributor scope, community intelligence study, harmful-information definition and crisis framing, staff-safety context, data transparency, and eight-pillar resilience roadmap.
